nal services, consultancy, and services procurement

Professional services Consultancy Services procurement (also known as SoW) Outsourced services

Resources are under the supervision, direction and control of the contracting authority No No No No

Resources are under the supervision, direction and control of supplier Usually, yes, although there are exceptions Yes Yes Yes

Specific deliverables outlined Yes Yes Yes Yes

Provides advice No Yes Usually, no Usually, no

Part of BAU service delivery Yes No It depends Yes

3. Examples

3.1. Consultancy

3.1.1. The buyer is a Government Department that is merging two legacy operational directorates. The buyer requires strategic advice outside of their existing organisational design and change management capability to map the end-to-end transformation. The consultancy is time limited and operates outside of the buyer’s headcount. The arrangement is for an approved set of deliverables and the supplier determines how this is done. To ensure effective knowledge transfer, the supplier provides any applicable toolkits, shares methodologies and process maps used and delivers upskilling workshops to the buyer’s staff to ensure lasting capability improvements within the buyer organisation and to reduce future reliance on external resources.

3.1.2. The buyer could commission the requirement on a time and materials basis, however best value would be achieved by utilising an output based pricing methodology. To do this effectively the buyer will need a detailed specification which may result in the requirement being split into a discovery phase followed by outputs. Alternatively, detailed market engagement will need to be undertaken to draft a specification that enables suppliers to understand the requirement and commit to output based pricing.

3.2. Contingent labour

3.2.1. A hiring manager in the local city council is responsible for recruiting a temporary worker to cover the role and responsibilities for maternity leave cover. Their organisation will have a recommended route for sourcing this requirement, and it will involve a CV sift and interviews to select the best candidate. The worker is brought in for a period of time, employed by the agency and under the supervision, direction and control of the council. The council pays a fixed hourly or daily rate for a worker that covers their pay, statutory costs, and a fee to the supplier for provision. If the worker wishes to take annual leave, then this is managed between the worker and their line manager at the council - the council pays only for the days that the worker actually is present in work. The worker will be expected to abide by the council’s policies and attend all staff calls.

3.3. Resource augmentation

3.3.1. The buyer has a requirement for experienced software specialists to assist the implementation of a new enterprise resource planning system and has contracted with a supplier who will provide them with the resource for an agreed period of time. The buyer has communicated an agreed project budget but the supplier will share the workers’ day rates. The intention is to help speed up the deployment and upskilling of the permanent staff on the team. There is a plan to work to, and they are under the direction and control of the buyer, meaning the buyer sets the pace and direction of work. One of the specialists doesn’t fit with the culture of the organisation so the buyer requests another resource of equal calibre from the supplier. Another specialist has time off coming up, notifies the buyer, but it’s the supplier who grants and manages this, considering if the gap needs to be covered. As the work progresses, the buyer and temporary staff can focus on knowledge transfer and upskilling. The supplier provides templates and training packs they’ve previously delivered and is able to share their best practice when implementing complex back office software. Under a typical provision of contingent labour, the supplier taking responsibility for replacing the worker, granting annual leave, and providing knowledge transfer would not be expected to happen.

3.4. Professional services

3.4.1. A buying organisation submits itself to annual auditing. The supplier is responsible for auditing the organisation’s financial affairs and must produce an output outlining the success and effectiveness of their governance controls, as well as provide recommendations for increasing compliance with financial rules and regulations. The work has been agreed at a fixed price. The supplier deploys a team of auditors into the organisation to review paperwork, practices and interview staff, but they do not sit within an existing team.

3.5. Services procurement and SoW

3.5.1. A buyer has a requirement to develop a comprehensive platform to provide guidance and training material on a new policy area that will be launched to the public in six months. The buyer does not feel strongly about how this is done, instead is focused on a successful outcome, providing it is compliant with accessibility and marketing and communications guidance. The buyer contracts the supplier to be responsible for the delivery of this outcome. The buyer defines milestones and acceptance criteria for agreement by the supplier, linked to payment terms. The supplier delivers the requirement on time, and to the agreed quality.
